q: Judging a product's profitability on the results of a single year can mislead, and life-cycle costing corrects this, mainly because:

options.A: A product never incurs any cost before the year of its launch
options.B: Costs and revenues of a product follow different patterns over its life — heavy development and launch costs fall in the early years, while the bulk of the revenue may come later
options.C: Annual accounts are not prepared for individual products at all
options.D: The selling price of a product remains unchanged throughout its life

q: For a durable asset such as a locomotive, life-cycle costing supports the purchase decision by comparing offers on the basis of:

options.A: The initial purchase price alone, the lowest offer being preferred
options.B: The maintenance cost of the first year alone
options.C: The resale value expected at the end of its life alone
options.D: The total of purchase price, operating and maintenance costs over its working life and disposal cost, less any residual value

q:
Consider the following statements about throughput accounting:
1. Labour and overhead costs are treated as operating expenses of the period rather than being added to the cost of each unit of inventory.
2. Building up inventory is treated as a means of increasing profit for the period.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: A product gives a throughput of Rs 450 per unit and takes 0.3 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. The return per factory hour is:

options.A: Rs 135
options.C: Rs 450
options.D: Rs 150

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes throughput accounting from traditional absorption costing?

options.A: Throughput accounting adds labour and overheads to inventory values, while absorption costing does not
options.B: Throughput accounting values inventory at material cost only and discourages production merely to absorb overheads, while absorption costing values inventory at full production cost and can reward over-production
options.C: Absorption costing is based on the Theory of Constraints, while throughput accounting is not
options.D: There is no difference between the two in the valuation of inventory

q: Marginal costing is also called variable costing because, under this technique:

options.A: Only the fixed costs are charged to the products
options.B: Only the variable costs are charged to the products, the fixed costs being treated as costs of the period
options.C: The selling price of every product is kept variable
options.D: All costs are assumed to vary in direct proportion to output

q: The contribution earned by a business is applied, in order, towards:

options.A: Paying the dividend to the shareholders and then meeting the variable costs
options.B: Meeting the variable costs first and then the fixed costs
options.C: Creating reserves, the fixed costs being met out of capital
options.D: Meeting the fixed costs first, the balance remaining thereafter being the profit

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A product may give a positive contribution and yet the business as a whole may show a net loss, if the total contribution is less than the total fixed costs.
2. Net profit begins only when the total contribution exceeds the total fixed costs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: The P/V ratio is also known by the name of:

options.A: Contribution-to-sales ratio
options.B: Margin of safety ratio
options.C: Fixed cost recovery ratio
options.D: Profit-to-sales ratio

q: A product is sold at Rs 150 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 90 per unit. The total fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The break-even point in units is:

options.A: 2,400 units
options.B: 4,000 units
options.C: 6,000 units
options.D: 5,400 units

q: Which of the following actions will improve the P/V ratio of a product, other things remaining the same?

options.A: Increasing the total fixed costs of the business
options.B: Reducing the variable cost per unit of the product
options.C: Reducing the selling price per unit of the product
options.D: Increasing the variable cost per unit of the product

q: A business is said to break even at that level of sales at which:

options.A: The total sales value is equal to the total variable cost
options.B: The profit earned is the maximum possible
options.C: The margin of safety is equal to the total sales
options.D: The total revenue is exactly equal to the total cost, so that there is neither a profit nor a loss

q: The margin of safety, expressed in units, is worked out as:

options.A: The units actually (or budgeted to be) sold minus the break-even units
options.B: The break-even units minus the units actually sold
options.C: The total fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit
options.D: The units actually sold divided by the break-even units

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000 and its variable costs are Rs 7,20,000. Its P/V ratio is:
In break-even analysis, a wide angle of incidence at the break-even point indicates that:

options.A: Profit is earned only at a very slow rate after the break-even point is crossed
options.B: The fixed costs of the business are very high in relation to its sales
options.C: Profit is earned at a rapidly increasing rate once the break-even point is crossed, the margin on additional sales being high
options.D: The business can never earn a profit, whatever the volume of sales

q: In a break-even chart, the line showing the fixed cost is drawn parallel to the horizontal axis of the chart. This manner of drawing it indicates that:

options.A: The fixed cost per unit remains the same at every level of output
options.B: No fixed cost at all is incurred when the output is nil
options.C: The total fixed cost rises in direct proportion to the output
options.D: The total fixed cost remains the same in amount at every level of output, within the capacity installed

q: One of the basic assumptions of cost-volume-profit analysis is that:

options.A: The selling price per unit remains the same at all levels of output and sales
options.B: The selling price per unit falls as the volume of sales rises
options.C: The variable cost per unit rises steadily with every increase in output
options.D: The total fixed costs go on increasing in proportion to output

q: The fixed costs of an enterprise are Rs 4,80,000 and its P/V ratio is 30%. Its break-even sales are:
A recognised limitation of cost-volume-profit analysis is that it:

options.A: Cannot be used by a manufacturing concern at all
options.B: Takes no account of the fixed costs of the business
options.C: Assumes that the whole of the additional output can be sold at the existing price, ignoring that a reduction in price may be necessary to sell a larger volume
options.D: Requires the accounts of at least ten previous years before it can be applied

q: A factory is considering replacing an old machine. In evaluating the proposal, the depreciation charged every year on the machine already in use is:

options.A: A relevant cost, because it appears in the cost accounts
options.B: An opportunity cost of the replacement proposal
options.C: A differential cost between the two alternatives
options.D: Not a relevant cost, being a non-cash allocation of a cost already incurred in the past

q: Where one of the alternatives under consideration involves an additional fixed cost, such as the rent of extra premises, the differential cost of that alternative:

options.A: Includes that additional fixed cost, since differential cost is the change in total cost between the alternatives
options.B: Excludes it, because a fixed cost can never form part of differential cost
options.C: Is limited to the variable cost of one additional unit only
options.D: Is the same as the sunk cost of the alternative

q: An enterprise shows sales of Rs 4,00,000 with a profit of Rs 20,000 in one year and sales of Rs 6,00,000 with a profit of Rs 60,000 in the next year, its cost structure remaining unchanged. Its break-even sales are:
Apart from the comparison of costs, a make-or-buy decision must also take into account:

options.A: The book value of the machinery installed in the factory
options.B: Qualitative factors such as assurance of regular supply, control over the quality of the component and the alternative use of the capacity released
options.C: The total fixed overheads allocated to the component in the cost accounts
options.D: The price at which the finished product is sold to the customers

q: In comparing the cost of making a component with the price of buying it from outside, the fixed costs that will continue to be incurred under both the alternatives should be:

options.A: Added in full to the cost of making the component
options.B: Added in full to the purchase price quoted by the supplier
options.C: Divided equally between the two alternatives
options.D: Excluded from the comparison, as they do not differ between the alternatives

q: The decision whether to close down a plant temporarily during a period of slack demand is taken by comparing:

options.A: The loss that would be suffered if production continues with the loss that would be suffered if the plant is shut down, the latter including the unavoidable fixed costs and the extra costs of closing and re-opening
options.B: The total cost of production with the book value of the plant
options.C: The selling price of the product with its variable cost alone
options.D: The profit of the current year with the profit of the previous year

q: The actual sales of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its break-even sales are Rs 6,75,000. Its margin of safety is:
A firm working well below its capacity is offered a special order. In the short run, the lowest price it can accept for the order without suffering a loss on it is the price that covers:

options.A: The total cost of the product, including a full share of the fixed overheads
options.B: The incremental cost of executing the order, that is, its variable cost together with any extra cost caused by the order itself
options.C: The average cost of production of the previous year
options.D: The price charged to its regular customers for the same product

q: A limiting factor in production is a factor which:

options.A: Limits the profit that can be earned in any single year
options.B: Is always the shortage of finance in the business
options.C: Relates only to the selling activities of the enterprise
options.D: Restricts the volume of production or sales, such as a shortage of skilled labour, material or machine capacity, or a limited demand for the product

q: When a raw material is in short supply and has to be shared among several products, the products should be ranked for production according to:

options.A: The contribution earned per unit of the scarce material consumed by each product
options.B: The selling price of each product
options.C: The net profit shown by each product after allocation of all overheads
options.D: The total variable cost incurred on each product

q: A product is sold at Rs 90 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 54 per unit. The fixed costs are Rs 2,16,000. The number of units that must be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 1,08,000 is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 4,000 units
options.C: 9,000 units
options.D: 12,000 units

q: An important advantage claimed for marginal costing is that:

options.A: It values the closing stock at the full total cost of production
options.B: The profit of a period is not affected merely by producing more or less for stock, since fixed costs are charged against the revenue of the period in which they are incurred
options.C: It makes the separation of costs into fixed and variable elements unnecessary
options.D: It is accepted for the valuation of stock in the published financial accounts

q: For the purpose of external financial reporting, marginal costing suffers from the limitation that:

options.A: It charges the variable costs of production against the revenue of a later period
options.B: It requires the fixed costs to be capitalised as an asset
options.C: It ignores the variable cost of the goods remaining unsold
options.D: The closing stock is valued at the variable cost only, excluding the fixed production overheads, and is therefore understated as compared with the total cost of production

q: For applying break-even analysis to a concern whose costs include semi-variable items, the fixed and variable elements of such items are commonly separated by using:

options.A: The high-low method, which compares the total cost at the highest and the lowest levels of activity
options.B: The method of valuing the closing stock at the end of the period
options.C: The ratio of the current assets to the current liabilities
options.D: The rate of depreciation charged on the plant

q: The fixed costs of an enterprise are Rs 2,50,000 and its P/V ratio is 25%. The sales required to earn a desired profit of Rs 1,50,000 are:
If the sales mix of a multi-product firm shifts towards the products having a higher P/V ratio, the overall break-even point of the firm will:

options.A: Rise, because the total sales value increases
options.B: Remain completely unaffected by the change in the mix
options.C: Fall, because the weighted average P/V ratio of the firm improves
options.D: Become equal to the total fixed costs of the firm

q: If the variable cost per unit of a product rises, its selling price and the total fixed costs remaining unchanged, the break-even point of the firm will:

options.A: Fall, because the total cost of production rises
options.B: Remain exactly the same as before
options.C: Become nil, because no profit can then be earned
options.D: Rise, because the contribution per unit falls and more units must be sold to recover the fixed costs

q: The marginal cost of a product is made up of:

options.A: The prime cost plus the variable overheads
options.B: The prime cost plus the fixed factory overheads
options.C: The works cost plus the administration overheads
options.D: The direct material cost alone

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 15,00,000, its P/V ratio is 20% and its fixed costs are Rs 1,80,000. Its profit is:
A product line should be discontinued only when:

options.A: It shows a net loss after the allocation of the common fixed overheads
options.B: Its sales are lower than the sales of the other product lines
options.C: The fixed costs that would be saved by discontinuing it are greater than the contribution that would be lost by doing so
options.D: Its variable cost per unit is higher than that of any other product

q: A special order can be executed with the existing plant, but it requires a special die costing Rs 25,000 which will have no use afterwards. In deciding whether to accept the order, this cost of the die is:

options.A: A sunk cost, to be ignored in the decision
options.B: An imputed cost, involving no cash payment
options.C: A part of the general fixed overheads of the factory
options.D: A relevant incremental cost caused by the order, to be recovered from the price quoted for it

q: In a profit-volume chart, the slope of the line showing the profit or loss at different levels of sales represents the:

options.A: P/V ratio of the business
options.B: Total fixed costs of the business
options.C: Margin of safety of the business
options.D: Selling price per unit of the product

q: An enterprise desires a profit after tax of Rs 90,000. The rate of tax is 25%, its fixed costs are Rs 1,80,000 and its P/V ratio is 30%. The sales required to earn this profit are:

Consider the following statements:
1. The total fixed cost of a business is assumed to remain unchanged only within a given range of activity and an existing plant capacity.
2. When production is pushed beyond that capacity, the fixed costs may themselves increase, for example by the installation of additional plant.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: In a contribution (marginal costing) statement of profit, the profit of the period is arrived at by:

options.A: Deducting the variable cost of sales from the fixed costs
options.B: Adding the total contribution to the total fixed costs
options.C: Deducting the closing stock from the total cost of production
options.D: Deducting the total fixed costs, as one single block, from the total contribution earned on the goods sold

q: A firm sells two products: M with sales of Rs 5,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 20%, and N with sales of Rs 5,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 40%. Its total fixed costs are Rs 2,40,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
If the margin of safety of a business is nil, it means that the business:

options.A: Has earned the maximum profit possible on its sales
options.B: Is operating exactly at its break-even level, earning neither a profit nor a loss
options.C: Has no fixed costs to recover
options.D: Has sold nothing during the period

q: The actual sales of an enterprise are Rs 8,00,000, its break-even sales are Rs 5,00,000 and its P/V ratio is 40%. Its profit is:
The shut-down point of a plant is the level of output below which:

options.A: The variable cost per unit begins to rise
options.B: The firm starts earning a profit on its sales
options.C: The margin of safety of the firm becomes negative
options.D: It is more economical to close the plant down temporarily than to keep it working, because the loss on working would exceed the loss on shutting down

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 3,00,000 a year, out of which Rs 90,000 would still have to be incurred even if the plant is shut down. The contribution is Rs 35 per unit. The shut-down point is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 8,571 units
options.C: 2,571 units
options.D: 11,143 units

q: Break-even analysis is regarded mainly as a short-run tool of management because it:

options.A: Is prepared only for a period of one month
options.B: Rests on the existing plant capacity, cost structure, prices and efficiency, which cannot be assumed to hold good over a long period
options.C: Ignores the variable costs of production altogether
options.D: Can be applied only when the firm sells a single product

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 8,50,000. Its cash inflows are Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor 0.909), Rs 3,50,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor 0.826) and Rs 3,50,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor 0.751). Its Net Present Value is:
A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 18,000 at a discount rate of 12% and (-) Rs 12,000 at a discount rate of 15%. By interpolation, its Internal Rate of Return is approximately:
A project costing Rs 9,60,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,40,000 in Year 1, Rs 3,20,000 in Year 2, Rs 2,80,000 in Year 3 and Rs 3,00,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:

options.A: 3.4 years
options.B: 3.0 years
options.C: 2.4 years
options.D: 4.0 years

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 6,30,000. The discounted values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,80,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,10,000 in Year 2, Rs 1,90,000 in Year 3 and Rs 1,70,000 in Year 4. Its discounted payback period is approximately:

options.A: 2.29 years
options.B: 4.00 years
options.C: 3.00 years
options.D: 3.29 years

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 14,40,000 and its initial investment is Rs 12,00,000. Its Profitability Index is:

An investment of Rs 9,00,000 is expected to have a salvage value of Rs 1,00,000 at the end of its life and to yield an average annual profit after depreciation of Rs 65,000. Its Average Rate of Return on the average investment is:
A company issues debentures carrying interest at 10%. If the corporate tax rate is 30%, the after-tax cost of this debt is:
A company issues 11% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 110 per share. The shares are irredeemable. The cost of this preference capital is:

The expected dividend on a company's equity share is Rs 18 per share, its current market price is Rs 150 per share and dividends are expected to grow at 6% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
An enterprise is financed by 60% equity with a cost of 16% and 40% debt with an after-tax cost of 8%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:

A company expects a dividend of Rs 12 per equity share. The market price is Rs 100 per share, flotation costs on a new issue are 5% of the price, and dividends are expected to grow at 5% per year. The cost of a new equity issue is approximately:

Funds are limited and the competing independent projects are divisible. Project A requires Rs 4,00,000 and has a Net Present Value of Rs 80,000; Project B requires Rs 6,00,000 and has a Net Present Value of Rs 1,50,000; Project C requires Rs 5,00,000 and has a Net Present Value of Rs 90,000. Ranked by Profitability Index, the first priority should go to:

options.A: Project A, whose Profitability Index is 1.20
options.B: Project C, whose Profitability Index is 1.18
options.C: Project A, because it needs the least capital
options.D: Project B, whose Profitability Index is 1.25

q: In sensitivity analysis of a capital project, a variable is regarded as the most sensitive when:

options.A: It has the largest absolute value in the project estimates
options.B: A small percentage change in it produces the largest change in the project's Net Present Value
options.C: It is the last variable to be estimated by the project team
options.D: Its estimated value is the most certain of all the variables

q: The expected cash inflow of a project for a year is Rs 2,00,000 and its certainty-equivalent coefficient is 0.85. The present value factor at the risk-free rate for that year is 0.909. The present value of the certainty-equivalent inflow is:
A risky project is expected to give a cash inflow of Rs 5,00,000 at the end of one year. Evaluated at a risk-adjusted discount rate of 15%, the present value of this inflow is approximately:
In judging whether a railway work is remunerative, the rate of return is worked out, at the concept level, as:

options.A: The gross earnings of the work expressed as a percentage of its working expenses
options.B: The total earnings of the whole railway expressed as a percentage of the capital-at-charge
options.C: The working expenses of the work expressed as a percentage of its capital cost
options.D: The net incremental earnings of the work, after meeting its incremental working expenses, expressed as a percentage of its capital cost

q: A ranking conflict between the Net Present Value and the Internal Rate of Return for mutually exclusive projects arises primarily because the two methods differ in respect of:

options.A: The treatment of depreciation in the cash flows
options.B: The assumed rate at which intermediate cash inflows are reinvested, and the scale and timing of the projects
options.C: The treatment of the initial outlay in the first year
options.D: The inclusion of salvage value at the end of project life

q: A project is likely to show more than one Internal Rate of Return when its cash flow pattern is non-conventional, that is, when:

options.A: The initial outlay is recovered in the first year itself
options.B: All the cash inflows are equal in every year
options.C: The sign of the net cash flow changes more than once over the life of the project
options.D: The project has no salvage value at the end of its life

q: A project gives a uniform annual cash inflow and its payback period is 4 years. Where the life of the project is much longer than the payback period, the reciprocal of the payback period gives an approximate Internal Rate of Return of:
A project has a Net Present Value of Rs 4,56,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.800. Its equivalent annual annuity is:
A new machine costs Rs 7,50,000. The old machine it replaces is sold for Rs 1,20,000. Ignoring tax, the net initial cash outlay on the replacement is:

A project requires additional working capital at its commencement, which is expected to be recovered in full at the end of its life. In a discounted cash flow appraisal, this working capital should be treated as:

options.A: Ignored altogether, since it is not a capital cost of the project
options.B: A cash outflow at commencement, with no corresponding inflow at any stage
options.C: A cash outflow at commencement and a cash inflow, discounted, at the end of the project's life
options.D: An addition to the annual operating profit of every year of the project

q: A project costing Rs 4,80,000 with no salvage value yields total profits after depreciation of Rs 2,40,000 over its life of 4 years. Its Average Rate of Return on the average investment is:
For appraising a proposed new investment, the cost of capital that is conceptually most relevant is:

options.A: The historical average cost of the funds raised in the past
options.B: The cost of the cheapest source of finance ever used by the enterprise
options.C: The book cost of the existing capital shown in the balance sheet
options.D: The marginal cost of capital, that is, the cost of the new funds to be raised for the investment

q: Market-value weights are generally preferred to book-value weights in computing the weighted average cost of capital because they:

options.A: Are easier to obtain from the published accounts of the enterprise
options.B: Reflect the current values and the target financing proportions relevant to new investment decisions
options.C: Always give a lower weighted average cost of capital
options.D: Eliminate the need to estimate the cost of equity altogether

q: A company issues debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 96, carrying interest at 12% and redeemable at Rs 105 after 5 years. Ignoring tax, the approximate cost of this debt, taking the average of the issue price and the redemption value as the base, is approximately:

A project requires an outlay of Rs 10,00,000. The present value of its operating cash inflows is Rs 9,20,000, the present value of its salvage value is Rs 60,000 and the present value of the working capital to be recovered is Rs 45,000. Its Net Present Value is:
For one and the same project, where the discount rate is positive, the discounted payback period will ordinarily be:

options.A: Shorter than the simple payback period
options.B: Exactly half of the simple payback period
options.C: Unrelated to the simple payback period
options.D: Longer than, or at best equal to, the simple payback period

q: The Profitability Index may give a misleading choice between mutually exclusive projects of very different size, because:

options.A: It is computed without discounting the cash flows
options.B: Being a relative measure, it shows the return per rupee invested but not the total addition to wealth, which the Net Present Value shows
options.C: It can be computed only when the Internal Rate of Return is known
options.D: It ignores the salvage value of the project altogether

q: The present value of a project's cash inflows is Rs 8,00,000 and its Net Present Value is (+) Rs 80,000. The percentage by which the cash inflows can fall before the Net Present Value becomes zero is:
The financial break-even level of a project is the level of sales or output at which:

options.A: The Net Present Value of the project is zero, the cost of capital being fully recovered
options.B: The total contribution is exactly equal to the fixed costs only
options.C: The accounting profit of the project is at its maximum
options.D: The payback period of the project is the shortest possible

q: A project costing Rs 5,00,000 is expected to give a uniform cash inflow of Rs 1,50,000 a year for 5 years. The annuity factor required is 3.333, which lies close to the 5-year annuity factor at 15% (3.352). Its Internal Rate of Return is approximately:

A project gives earnings before interest, tax and depreciation of Rs 2,60,000. Depreciation is Rs 60,000 and the tax rate is 25% on the profit after depreciation. The annual cash inflow from the project is:
A project involves additional depreciation of Rs 1,60,000 a year and the tax rate is 30%. The annual depreciation tax shield of the project is:

options.D: Nil, since depreciation is a non-cash charge

q: A new product is expected to reduce the sales, and hence the contribution, of an existing product of the same enterprise. In appraising the new product, this loss of contribution on the existing product should be:

options.A: Treated as a relevant incremental cost and charged against the new product
options.B: Ignored, because it does not involve any cash payment to an outsider
options.C: Added to the expected contribution of the new product
options.D: Recorded only as a note, with no effect on the appraisal figures

q: Where the cash flows of a project have been estimated in real terms, that is, at constant prices without allowing for inflation, consistency in appraisal requires that they should be discounted at:

options.A: The nominal rate of discount, which includes the effect of inflation
options.B: The rate of inflation expected over the life of the project
options.C: A rate of discount of zero, since prices are held constant
options.D: The real rate of discount, from which the effect of inflation has been removed

q: The coefficient of variation is preferred to the standard deviation alone for comparing the risk of two projects with different expected returns because it measures:

options.A: The absolute dispersion of returns around the mean, in rupees
options.B: The risk per unit of expected return, being the standard deviation divided by the expected return
options.C: The probability that a project will make a loss
options.D: The range between the highest and the lowest possible return

q: In the certainty-equivalent approach, the coefficient applied to the expected cash inflow of a year will be lower when:

options.A: The cash inflow belongs to the first year of the project
options.B: The inflow is a salvage receipt at the end of the project
options.C: The expected inflow is judged to be more risky and less certain
options.D: The risk-free rate of interest is higher

q: A work may fail the test of financial remunerativeness and yet be taken up on safety, strategic or wider social considerations. Sound appraisal practice in such a case requires that:

options.A: The shortfall in the financial return should be explicitly brought out, so that the decision is taken with full knowledge of it
options.B: The earnings of the work should be suitably increased on paper until the test is passed
options.C: No rate of return should be computed for the work at all
options.D: The capital cost of the work should be charged to revenue to improve its return

q: 'Soft' capital rationing, as distinguished from 'hard' capital rationing, arises from:

options.A: An absolute inability of the enterprise to raise any funds from the market
options.B: A direction of the lenders that no new project should be undertaken
options.C: The closure of the capital market to all borrowers
options.D: Limits on capital expenditure imposed by the management itself as a matter of policy or prudence

q: In a lease-versus-buy appraisal of an asset, the comparison is properly made between:

options.A: The total lease rentals payable over the lease period and the purchase price of the asset, both undiscounted
options.B: The present value of the after-tax lease payments and the present value of the after-tax costs of owning the asset, including its salvage value
options.C: The annual lease rental and the annual depreciation charge on the asset
options.D: The book value of the asset and the security deposit payable under the lease

q: A project already in operation should be abandoned at a given stage when:

options.A: Its original capital cost has not yet been fully recovered through depreciation
options.B: Its accounting profit for the latest year is lower than in the previous year
options.C: The amount realisable on abandonment exceeds the present value of the cash flows expected from continuing it
options.D: A newer project with a higher rate of return becomes available anywhere in the enterprise

q: Where two mutually exclusive machines with different lives are to be compared on a continuing, repeatable basis, the replacement-chain (common-life) method proceeds by:

options.A: Repeating each machine over a common period equal to the least common multiple of their lives, and comparing the Net Present Values over that common period
options.B: Comparing only the first life of each machine, regardless of the difference in lives
options.C: Adding the salvage values of the two machines and dividing by their combined life
options.D: Rejecting the machine with the shorter life in all cases

q: Traditional discounted cash flow appraisal tends to understate the true worth of a flexible project because it does not separately value:

options.A: The salvage value expected at the end of the project's life
options.B: The working capital to be recovered on completion of the project
options.C: The depreciation tax shield arising during the project's life
